newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Pro-Beijing HK politician wants electoral change.
newsitem.headline: Pro-Beijing HK politician wants electoral change.

text.p: The leader of Hong Kong's largest pro-Beijing political party demanded on Sunday the scrapping of the first-past-the-post electoral system that benefitted Hong Kong's Democratic Party in the 1995 polls.

Tsang Yok-sing, chairman of the Democratic Alliance for the Betterment of Hong Kong (DAB), which won six seats in the 60-member Legislative Council, slammed the system as unfair and called for proportional representation instead.
The Democrats, Hong Kong's largest party chaired by lawyer Martin Lee, won 19 seats in the council that China will dissolve when it resumes sovereignty of Hong Kong in 19 week's time.

Beijing plans to replace the elected legislature, returned under democratic reforms introduced by colonial Governor Chris Patten and opposed by China, with an appointed provisional legislature until new elections are called.

"Under this (first-past-the-post) system, the number of seats won by a party does not necessarily reflect the amount of support it gets from the voters," Tsang said in Hong Kong Radio's weekly "Letter from Hong Kong" broadcast.

"The DAB favours a proportional representation system which awards each party a number of seats that matches the proportion of votes he gets," said Tsang, a 49-year-old headmaster who failed to win election in 1995.
"This system is arguably more fair than first-past-the-post. At any rate, it is no less democratic."

Under the first-past-the-post system, the candidate that receives the most votes in each district wins the seat. Under proportional representation, voters rank their choices and the secondary votes also count.
Tsang was appointed to the provisional legislature and to key China-supervised committees responsible for the transition.
The Democrats have been cold-shouldered by China and in turn boycotted China's panels that chose Hong Kong's future leader, Tung Chee-hwa, denouncing the bodies as travesties of democracy.
Senior Chinese officials overseeing Hong Kong's handover have previously said they expect the territory to hold its first post-handover democratic election in 1998.
